description: Hi! We are Trencalòs, an engineering team passionate about Space.
summary: A web app with 3D globes of Mars, the Moon and Earth: click any point of Mars or the Moon and it finds the places on Earth that are physically most similar, using NASA data compared in physical units, cell by cell. It also tells you where on Earth each part of a rover could be field-tested, and finds Earth paths with the same slopes as a rover traverse.
details:
WHAT DOES IT DO?

Before we build on the Moon or Mars, we rehearse on Earth, but today the rehearsal site is usually picked by habit. Earth Analogs is a web app with 3D globes of Mars, the Moon and Earth. Click any point of Mars or the Moon (or of Earth) and the app scores every place of the other body, paints the globe by similarity, flies to the best match and shows a card with every variable, its value on both sides and its NASA source, plus an analog index from 0 to 100 broken down by dimension: terrain, thermal, water & ice, and sky & light. You can choose what you want to test (wheels, navigation, ice detection, solar power, dust, communications…) and restrict the search to a region of Earth.

It has two more views:

- Rover test planner: send a rover (NASA's Perseverance 3D model) to the clicked Mars or Moon cell and see, part by part, where on Earth it can be field-tested, where only with caveats, and what can only be tested in a lab (for example, anything that needs vacuum), plus the fewest sites that cover the whole rover.

- Route replica: draw a route on Mars or the Moon, or load a real rover traverse, and find on Earth a path with the same sequence of slopes.

HOW DOES IT WORK?

Each body is covered by equal-area hexagonal cells (Mars 2.0 million cells of ~9 km, the Moon 288,000 of ~12 km, Earth 14.1 million of ~6.5 km, of which 1.37 million deserts, polar ice and arid land are searched). Every cell has a card computed from NASA mission data at the same scale on every body (slope and roughness from ~460 m pixels on all three), so the comparison is fair. Each variable is compared in physical units with a soft note, the notes are averaged by dimension with the weights of the chosen test, and the ranking rewards homogeneous areas. Variables with no data are not compared, and the app says how many were used. Everything is pre-computed once into small files and the matching runs in the browser in under a second: there is no server. On Mars the card also shows the slope at the clicked point (~0.9 km), the solar energy for a horizontal panel and the mean wind and wind stress.

WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?

It turns the choice of an analog site from habit into a transparent, data-driven search over the whole planet, and it is honest about the limits: it shows what Earth cannot reproduce (gravity, vacuum) and which variables could not be compared. Mission and instrument teams can see what they can test where, and what they cannot test anywhere on Earth.

WHAT DO YOU HOPE TO ACHIEVE?

To help pick better and less obvious analog sites for testing rovers, instruments and operations before they fly. Our next step: use the Earth twins of Mars to learn when a rover's "no traces of past life found" really means something, and when it only means our instruments cannot see well enough (docs/NEXT_STEPS.md).

WHAT TOOLS DID YOU USE?

JavaScript with CesiumJS (3D globes), three.js (3D rover), Uber H3 (hexagonal grid) and Vite; Python (NumPy, pandas, h3, SciPy, h5py, rasterio) to process the data. Data: NASA PDS (MOLA, TES, Mars Odyssey GRS, MRO MCS, LOLA, Diviner, Lunar Prospector), SWIM 2.0, the NASA Ames Mars Global Climate Model, NASA Earthdata (MODIS, GPM IMERG, MERRA-2, ECOSTRESS), NOAA ETOPO 2022, and live imagery from NASA GIBS and NASA Solar System Treks.
